blocks.text: 4. Self Supervision From Raw Text
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446291807-948967073.png
This connects back to the single task formulation, already covered in this topic. Any genuinely raw block of text already contains its own correct answers.
The genuinely next word in the actual text is genuinely always the correct label for that position, a genuinely elegant, self-supervised setup explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.content: This self-supervision, already covered in this topic, directly explains why large language models can train on massive amounts of unlabeled internet text, without needing any human to manually annotate a single example.

blocks.text: 5. Sliding Prediction Windows
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446291807-331932928.png
This connects back to self-supervision from raw text, already covered in this topic. One genuinely single passage of text genuinely produces one training example per token position.

Every genuinely prefix of the passage genuinely becomes its own separate next-token prediction problem, a genuinely efficient reuse of the exact same passage explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Recapping Cross Entropy Loss

This connects back to the probability distribution over the vocabulary, already covered generally in Sampling. Training genuinely compares the predicted distribution against the true next token using cross-entropy loss.
This genuinely pushes probability mass toward the actual correct token at every single position, the exact loss function explored throughout the rest of this topic's own worked example.
7. Scaling To Massive Datasets
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446291808-952184836.png

This connects back to sliding prediction windows, already covered in this topic. Because genuinely every single token position is its own training example, raw text genuinely scales into billions of examples.

This genuinely massive scale is exactly what lets large language models train on genuinely enormous datasets, a genuinely direct consequence of the self-supervision already covered earlier in this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates generating training examples from a single passage, already covered as sliding prediction windows in this topic.

code.content:
text = "the cat sat on the mat".split()  # already covered as raw text in this topic

# already covered as sliding prediction windows in this topic
training_examples = []
for i in range(1, len(text)):
    input_prefix = text[:i]
    target = text[i]
    training_examples.append((input_prefix, target))

print("Training examples from one passage (already covered in this topic):")
for input_prefix, target in training_examples:
    print(f"  input={input_prefix} -> predict next token: '{target}'")

print(f"\nTotal training examples from this one short sentence (already covered as scaling to massive datasets in this topic): {len(training_examples)}")

# already covered as recapping cross entropy loss in this topic
predicted_probs = {"mat": 0.6, "rug": 0.25, "floor": 0.15}
true_token = "mat"
loss = -1 * (predicted_probs[true_token] ** 0)  # simplified illustration, not real cross-entropy math
print(f"\nModel predicted probability for the true next token '{true_token}' (already covered in this topic): {predicted_probs[true_token]}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Next token prediction is the single, simple training objective behind large language models.
Given every token seen so far, the model predicts which vocabulary token comes next.
Raw text already contains its own correct answers, making this a self-supervised task.
One passage of text produces one training example per token position, a sliding window.
Cross-entropy loss compares the predicted distribution against the true next token during training.
Because every token position is its own example, raw text scales into billions of training examples.
After training, the same prediction ability gets reused, one step at a time, to generate new text.
This self-supervision needs no manually labeled data, a major reason for its power at scale.
Next up: Context Window, exploring how much text a model can actually condition on at once.
